grammar.note_en:
へ marks direction toward a place: ここからえきへいきます means “I go from here toward the station.” Write the particle へ but read it e. It follows the destination or direction, as in みぎへいきます, “go to the right.” まっすぐ is an adverb: まっすぐいきます, “go straight.” These are complete polite statements, not imperatives. The characters use statements of their own next actions to coordinate their route.

から marks the starting point, while まで marks the endpoint: かわからかどまでかえります means “return from the river as far as the corner.” The two endpoints identify the actual route; reversing them changes the journey. A direction can be given with へ without presenting it as the endpoint of a from–as far as pair. This chapter does not teach causal から, which has a later introduction.

で marks the place at which an action happens. へやでおしらせをかきます means “write a notice in the room”; えきでおしらせをよみます means “read a notice at the station.” Contrast めいはへやにいます, “Mei is in the room.” に marks the location of her presence there, whereas で marks the setting of writing. Do not replace every earlier に with で. A clock time still takes に, as in さんじはんにしまります, “closes at3:30.” Writing on a field or card also retains the already taught receiving-surface に with かきます.

In えきでかぎのかかりにあいます, “meet the person responsible for the key at the station,” で gives the setting and に marks the person met. The whole polite surface あいます is already taught; this chapter makes its bounded meeting partner explicit. かかり is the person responsible for a task. かぎのかかり identifies that person’s responsibility, not a newly named character. Asking someone a question can be expressed by the already taught ききます followed by the direct spoken question.

まで also gives a time endpoint: さんじはんまでへやにいます means “remain in the room until3:30.” Compare さんじはんにしまります, “closes at3:30.” Until gives the span’s endpoint; at gives the clock time of an event. しまります is the scheduled closing of the room/facility, not a command to close a door. Today's closing and tomorrow's gathering happen on different days even though both clock times are3:30 p.m. No new past tense or negative existence form is being taught.

いきます means go; きます means come toward the speaker or the place treated as the conversation’s centre; かえります means return to a place already associated with the traveller. Mei asks whether the volunteers will come back to her room. Later Ren describes the caretaker’s promised visit from the reading-room viewpoint. Do not substitute these solely because English sometimes translates all three as movement. Each surface is taught whole; there is no licence to infer untaught verb forms.

The public shop memo uses へ for its addressee, ほんのへやへ, “To the reading room,” and から for its sender, かぎのかかりから, “From the person responsible for the key.” These bounded uses extend the direction/source contrast; they do not introduce quotative と or a private letter. The memo is displayed with the shop’s public notices and stays there. Yui copies its morning information onto her own separate large card. Her copy is not a third invitation. The note gives tomorrow morning’s visit but does not locate the key or solve today's closing deadline.

The story now shows five kanji characters in four known spellings. Their readings remain visible: book, name, big and small retain their existing meanings. A whole lexical reading may cover the full word, including its kana ending. Every occurrence is annotated; recognition without the reading is optional. Exercises, vocabulary citations and card fronts stay kana in this phase. The original misleading map is corrected by cancelling its wrong labels before the new labels are treated as active; the delivered diagram shows that physical correction.
